{"docket_number": "53", "additional_docket_numbers": null, "term": "1968", "first_party": "Harold Kaufman ", "first_party_label": "Petitioner", "second_party": "United States", "second_party_label": "Respondent", "manner_of_jurisdiction": "Writ of certiorari", "lower_court": "United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit", "argued": ["1968-11-19T06:00:00Z"], "question": "

Can a federal prisoner challenge unlawfully-seized evidence in a post-conviction proceeding?

", "facts_of_the_case": "

During his trial for armed robbery of a federally insured savings and loan association, Harold Kaufman admitted to the crime but unsuccessfully claimed insanity. He was convicted and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit affirmed. Kaufman then filed a post-conviction motion in district court challenging the evidence that proved his sanity. He alleged that the evidence was unlawfully seized in violation of the Fourth Amendment. The district court denied relief, holding that unlawful search and seizure was not an available attack in post-conviction proceedings. The Eighth Circuit affirmed.

", "conclusion": "

Yes. Justice William J. Brennan, writing for a 5-3 majority, reversed and remanded. The Supreme Court held that Kaufman could challenge unlawfully seized evidence in a post-conviction proceeding. There was no need to show special circumstances. The fact that Kaufman admitted to the crime was irrelevant because he claimed an affirmative defense.

Justice Hugo L. Black dissented, arguing that prisoners can only challenge evidence post-conviction in special circumstances. The prisoner should have to cast some shadow of doubt on his guilt. Justice John M. Harlan wrote a separate dissent, writing that Kaufman did not show special circumstances, so should not be allowed to challenge the evidence post conviction. Justice Potter Stewart joined in the dissent. Justice Thurgood Marshall did not participate.

analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "I can hear your argument. All right, sir. Earlier, in discussing the facts, I mentioned that the appellate attorney who had been appointed to represent Kaufman as direct appeal failed to raise the search and seizure issue, and that Kaufman had requested him to raise the issue late, that the attorney had gone to the clerk, the clerk advised him that there was no formal way of raising the issue at that point, that the issue had been raised informally, however, by means of a letter, but even so, the court did not consider the issue, or apparently didn't consider it, because the opinion was silent on the issue. We feel, or we believe, that the advice of the clerk was misleading and improper. We feel that there, we believe that there were formal ways of raising this issue, even after oral argument. The attorney could have filed a supplemental brief together with a motion for leave to file a supplemental brief, or an amended brief together with a motion for leave to file an amended brief, or he could have filed an extraordinary motion to be allowed to re-argue the case. So, therefore, the clerk's advice was somewhat misleading. Under all of these circumstances, we contend that the defendant's right to appeal on this one issue was unconstitutionally frustrated, based on denial of the right to effective representation under the Sixth Amendment, based on the denial of the statutory right to appeal on this one question, the question of whether or not illegally seized evidence had been improperly used against him, and also we feel that due process was denied him through the conduct of the clerk and this whole set of circumstances. Mr. Jacob, isn't that pretty much just practicing law by ear, when lawyers go to the clerk and ask him what the procedures are, and then claim to rely on what he tells them instead of doing their own homework? Your Honor, the attorney should have known that there were formal ways to, I think if he had discussed this with other lawyers or had done some research, he would have found that there were formal ways of raising the question. I agree that he should have. He should not have relied entirely on the advice of the clerk, but apparently he did. I don't think he should have, however. The strict rule of the Eighth Circuit, as we've already contended, is an incorrect rule of law, and it should not have been applied by the trial court in denying Kaufman any relief on his search and seizure grounds. We also contend that even if this could be considered by this court to be a valid rule of law, in other words, even if this court should feel or should find that that the strict rule of the Eighth Circuit is constitutional, is a correct rule of law. We believe that Kaufman, at the very least, should have been given a delayed or out-of-time appeal on this one issue, the issue of whether or not illegally seized evidence had been improperly used against him. We've cited cases in our brief from the Fifth Circuit, the Boroff case, Lyles case, in which defendants have been frustrated in their attempts to appeal, and courts have given them delayed appeals or out-of-time appeals. And we feel that Kaufman should have had at least an out-of-time appeal on this one issue, should have had an out-of-time direct appeal on the issue of whether or not illegally seized evidence was improperly used against him. The facts in the record show that the search of Kaufman's person and the search of his car were illegal, that the evidence was improperly admitted, that the attorney adequately raised the issue at the trial, and also that the introduction of the evidence and the use of the evidence by the prosecutor did not constitute harmless error. These are the facts surrounding the search of the person and the search of the car. After the robbery, shortly after the robbery in St. Louis, or in the St. Louis area, a policeman in Alton, Illinois, which is across the Mississippi River from the St. Louis area, received a call to be on the lookout for a red rambler, which had been involved in a hit-and-run accident on the St. Louis side of the river. Shortly after he received this call, a red rambler came chugging across the bridge. The policeman followed the car. The car attempted to make a turn up a hill. It skidded on the ice, jumped up over the curb, and hit a tree. Kaufman was the driver of the car. The patrolman arrested Kaufman at that point for reckless driving, for driving too fast for conditions. The car was towed to a private garage. Kaufman was taken to police headquarters, the Alton police headquarters. His person was searched, and in the search of his person, the police found an auto rental contract showing that the red rambler had been rented to a person named Arthur Cooper. Also, the police found some of the proceeds of the robbery, $350 or $320, which had been taken during the robbery of the savings and loan. At about the same time, the time sequence is difficult to determine from the record, but at about the same time, the private garage owner found a pistol, a revolver in the back seat of the car, and he called the police and told them about it. They sent someone down to pick it up. The FBI then arrived at the Alton police station. They were given the products of this search of Kaufman's person, the auto rental contract, and the money. They then interrogated Kaufman, and he apparently made a full confession. Due to the time sequence, due to the fact that the evidence had been taken from his person before the interrogation, I think it's reasonable to assume, although the record is not altogether clear on this, it's reasonable to assume that Kaufman may have been induced to make this statement to the FBI because of the fact that the evidence had been found on his person, the evidence of the crime had been found on his person. The proceeds of the illegal search of the person then and the statement of Kaufman, plus the fact that the pistol, the revolver, had been found in the back seat of the car, plus the fact that Kaufman, shortly after the robbery, had been involved in a hit-and-run accident leaving Missouri and entering Illinois, constituted the probable cause, if the FBI had probable cause, for the search of the car. The search of the car did not actually take place until four and a half hours after the arrest. At this time, Kaufman had not been formally charged with any federal crime. Custody, at this time, had been transferred to the FBI, and they had taken Kaufman to St. Louis, to FBI headquarters there. At this point, two new FBI men went to the garage in Alton. They had no warrant, and they made a thorough search of the car. They spent two hours in searching the car and found a number of items, including a traffic ticket from New York City, some gasoline receipts showing that the car had driven through Pennsylvania, and a Western Union receipt showing that Kaufman had wired some money to his girlfriend in New York while he had been traveling through Pennsylvania. You referred to the search of his person as the illegal search. I think they're both illegal, Your Honor. When was he arrested? He was arrested at 445. Yes. He was taken immediately to the police station. His car was immediately hauled to the private garage, and the search took place apparently very shortly after 5 o'clock. While he was in the police station under arrest? That's right. Isn't it necessary for them to make some search of the person when they get in the police station? Well, this was not an ordinary inventory of the contents of his pockets conducted by the desk sergeant. This was a search. There were three or four policemen involved in the search. I think it's apparent from the record that this search was for the purpose of discovering evidence of the robbery. And the search had nothing to do with the arrest for reckless driving. There was no connection between the two. This was a search. It was not merely an inventory of the contents of his pockets. And the search was made at a great distance away from the car sometime after the arrest, so it cannot be considered a search incident to an arrest. Do you think the search is limited to, should be limited to what he has in his pockets? Well, I think the police could have frisked him for weapons, but this isn't what they did. They actually searched his pockets and were searching for evidence. I suppose they didn't want him to have those clothes if they had narcotics in them or some other things that are prohibited in prisons. Don't they have the right to do that when they're under arrest? If this was the purpose, I think the search... Pardon? If this was the purpose of the search of his person, I think the search would be valid. If the purpose was to inventory the contents of his pockets or to change clothes or put on a prison uniform or something for some reason such as that, I think the search would be justified. But I don't think that was the case here. The record indicates that this was a search, pure and simple, for evidence of the robbery. So we believe that the search of the person... Would you say they could have gotten a warrant with the search? Well, this would have... If they had gotten a warrant, certainly the search would have been more justified than it was under these circumstances. What do you think about getting a warrant? Was there probable cause? At this point, I don't think there was. No, at this point... You mean there wasn't any probable cause to arrest? Well, there was probable cause to arrest for reckless driving, but there was no probable cause to arrest for a crime such as robbery, robbery of the savings and loan. This time, all they had was suspicion concerning the robbery. They didn't have probable cause concerning the robbery of the savings and loan. We believe that this case, or the facts of our case, are much closer to the facts of the Preston case than they are to the facts of Cooper v. California, which the Solicitor General relies upon, and we have developed this fully in our brief. The defense attorney did not move to suppress this evidence prior to trial. At the trial, he objected to the auto rental contract, the money which had been obtained in the search of Kaufman's person, and to these four pieces of paper, the receipts and the Western Union receipt, the New York traffic ticket. He objected to all of these things. In fact, he moved to exclude the evidence taken during the search of Kaufman's person. He did not, however, make a motion to suppress prior to trial. The judge considered the objections on their merits, however, and ruled upon each objection. At the time, the judge ruled on the merits of these objections. There was sufficient evidence in the transcript to allow the judge to rule on the validity of these searches. If he failed to object or to make a motion to suppress to any particular item of evidence, would you still contend that he could raise it on 2255? I would say not, unless it could be considered incompetency of counsel or inadequacy of counsel, unless this were the reason why he did not object. No, no. But you say that here he objected to everything. Well, he didn't object to everything. He did not object to the gun. So that the gun is in evidence properly. That's right. I mean, not properly, but you can't object to it now. That's right. Our argument as to the gun is very, extremely weak. But as to the items which he did object to, I think we have a valid argument. I'd like to reserve some time to rebut. You may, Mr. Mr. Martin. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the court, this petition brings before the court an order of the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals, which dismissed a petitioner's appeal as frivolous. Therefore, there is no guiding light from the opinion as to on what ground the court decided the case. It didn't even permit him to lodge an appeal, isn't that correct? That's correct. It denied former porpoise, which I think under the standards articulated by this court we'd have to consider that the court determined that the appeal was frivolous. The district court first denied... That's correct. The district court adjudicated the merits of his claim that the taking of the drug during trial may have been competent at that time, and then said of the search and seizure claim that reviewing the record it was without merit, and at all events it could not be raised on collateral attack. And then with respect to the appeal, the attempted appeal, the district court first denied... That's right. ...the petition to appeal in former paupress, and that was followed by a similar denial by the court. That's correct. The only thing that the court did say in its order was that it had reviewed the entire record in this case. And I think that is important because I think that there are three separate grounds on which this court could affirm the decision of the circuit court, the denial of the petition here. That is one that at all events, even if we assume that the claim of search and seizure was good that the search was illegal, even if we assume that 2255 is a proper way to raise such a claim, a review of the record in this case will clearly establish that any error in the admission of this evidence was clearly harmless error under the standards that this court has enunciated. In Chapman v. California, the court rejected a rule that any constitutional error had to be considered harmful and reiterated its articulation of the harmless error rule in Fahey v. Connecticut that the question is whether there is a reasonable possibility that the evidence complained of might have contributed to the conviction. I think another way of looking at it is if the evidence had been excluded, is there a reasonable possibility that the jury might have reached a different result? We would submit that in this case, an examination of the record shows that there is no possibility that the jury would have reached a different result had this evidence of which petitioner now complains been excluded. In argument at more length than brief, counsel for petitioner has developed a theory on which this evidence that was seized may have had some bearing on the only defense raised to trial, the insanity defense. The petitioner never contested the commission of the crime. Petitioner says that this evidence was used by the government to show that the petitioner acted rationally on the day of the crime and that that fact, that he acted rationally, undermined his defense of insanity. I think the basic weakness in that position is found in the fact that the insanity defense at trial was not based on a claim that the defendant was irrational on the day he committed the crime, but rather that he was acting pursuant to an irresistible impulse. And indeed, petitioner's trial counsel argued that the fact that he behaved rationally on the day in question had no bearing on that. And I would refer the court to page 129 of the appendix. This is the summation of petitioner's trial counsel, appears approximately halfway down the page in the middle of the second full paragraph. And he said to the jury, We know that unlike some other mental illnesses, the intellect is not impaired. Changes can be schizophrenic, paranoid type. The person is still able to reason in this particular illness. He is not rendered conspicuous so that walking down the street, anyone can point and say, there is a schizophrenic paranoid. That doesn't mean that he is in control of his action. So this was the theory of the defense, that petitioner could appear to be totally rational at the time he committed the offense, and yet still be driven by an irresistible impulse to commit the crime. We therefore submit that this error, the admission of this evidence, could not possibly have infected that defense. We would point out further, if the court please, that the evidence that petitioner behaved in a rational manner is overwhelming in this case. First, the petitioner went into the bank in question. And was in the bank for approximately 20 minutes before he actually pulled out a gun and announced that this was a stick-up. He first went to a teller and discussed the purchase of traveler's checks, whether he could give a personal check to purchase traveler's checks, whether he could take out a loan to purchase them. He then had a discussion with another bank employee concerning the taking out of a loan. Their testimony indicates that during this entire period of 20 minutes in which he was in the bank, petitioner was entirely rational so that their evidence alone establishes that petitioner was acting rationally on that day. In addition, the FBI agents who interviewed petitioner on that night, one of whom was with petitioner for approximately four hours, testified that all during that time a petitioner was totally coherent, responded to questioning, and gave no indication of any irrationality. This was confirmed by several of the other people who interviewed petitioner on the night of his arrest. So the evidence was, as I said, overwhelming that petitioner was behaving rationally on the day in question. Further, I would point to the fact that petitioner's counsel presently argues that this evidence may have led the government to the fact that the petitioner traveled from New York to St. Louis to commit this crime that he made stops along the way. However, that information was also available to the government absent any of the items seized because the record establishes through the testimony of Agent Pete who interviewed petitioner on that evening that petitioner fully told the agents everything about his activities on the day of and prior to the robbery. At page 95 of the appendix, this was on a hearing outside the presence of the jury. Agent Pete gives a rather extensive summary of what petitioner told him on that day mentioning the fact that he traveled from St. Louis, from New York to St. Louis for the purpose of committing a robbery, that he stopped in Alton, Illinois on December 16th the same day of the robbery and purchased a gun, that he also purchased a holster and some ammunition, the route he traveled, et cetera, so that all of these facts were also otherwise available to the government. Now, I submit when this record is viewed in its totality, it is clear that any error in the admission of these few items that were seized from petitioner's person at the time of his arrest when he was in custody and from the car subsequently would clearly be harmless error under the standards articulated by this court. Having said that, I would like to turn to the question which petitioner has argued at some length and that is the question whether or not the claim of illegal search and seizure is one which can be raised on habeas corpus or its statutory counterpart, a 2255 motion. And we would, of course, draw no distinction between the two types of remedies, habeas corpus or 2255. In Sunwell v. Lodge, this court decided that the remedy of habeas corpus was not available to test issues that could have been raised at trial and on appeal at least where those, where the error complained of was not of constitutional proportion. The court did note that in some cases even where constitutional claims had been raised they had been denied where there was appellate relief available. We also recognize as did the court in Sunwell v. Lodge that there will be exceptional circumstances where even though as a general rule you might say the 2255 would not lie, exceptional circumstances may make it appropriate for the court to provide the remedy of a habeas corpus proceeding. We would submit that even when the questions are constitutional, there are strong policy considerations why prisoners should not be allowed to raise collaterally matters that they could have raised at the trial or on the direct appeal. We will also submit Mr. Martin, that argument isn't rested on any language of 2255. No, it is not. The language of 2255 by its terms at least indicates that the precise claims that he's pressing here are the constitutional ones. That's right. Our Congress won't be told. Our Congress. I think that basically it is a question as you mentioned before Mr. Justice Brennan of discretion. In what instances does the 2255 court go to the merits of the claim advanced? Now, it is our submission that there are certain constitutional issues which could be raised at trial that should not ordinarily be heard on a 2255 motion. We recognize at the same time that there are others that so basically go to the fairness of the original proceeding that even though they could have been raised, Well, do you think the test we've had in Fair Noir on the availability of the federal habeas remedy to state prisoners and the extent to which discretion is to be applied by the federal habeas judge, do you think those tests are equally serviceable in the 2255 area? I think that they are serviceable. I think they're a different consideration somewhat in the fact that I think your opinion may annoy us. There are different considerations, but I'm just wondering, we did say there that there are circumstances, although it's a federal constitutional claim, when a federal habeas judge is justified in refusing to entertain it. That's right. Now, what I'm wondering is, can we have a counterpart here in 2255 or are we going to have to fashion standards here different from those that we've fashioned for federal habeas? Well, I think certain things have to be taken into consideration that are different. I think your opinion in fey and noia for the court makes clear that one of the purposes of the federal habeas corpus statute for state prisoners was to make available a federal forum for the litigation of a prisoner's federal claims. It seems to me that that federal forum has been provided here, and I think that makes a very clear distinction between the two situations. I think also that basically some of those considerations are the same. We would suggest that to start from a general rule without talking for a moment about the exceptional circumstances, that there is a balancing of interest to be considered normally in a habeas corpus proceeding when a prisoner asserts denial of a constitutional right. There is society's interest in the finality of the judgment, and there is the prisoner's interest in the adjudication of his claim. Now, the question basically, as we would present it, would be which constitutional issues are such that they should be considered on 2255, regardless of the availability of direct appeal to have handled those issues, and those that should not. And we would suggest to the court that a useful analogy in solving this problem in the general terms is provided by this court's decisions in the cases involving the retroactive application of newly articulated constitutional principles. In those cases, the court has recognized that the new constitutional principle should be applied retroactively if it, and to use the words of the court in Roberts v. Russell, if the constitutional error presents a serious risk that the issue of guilt or innocence may not have been reliably determined. On the other hand, in the retroactivity cases, the court has recognized that where the constitutional principle does involve the reliability of the fact-finding process, the principle should not be applied retroactively. We submit also that where on a 2255 proceeding or habeas corpus, taken some time after the conviction, the court should not generally allow the assertion of even constitutional claims that could have been raised on direct appeal or at the original trial, unless the constitutional claim raised is one that seriously throws into question the reliability of the fact-finding process. We submit that the case presently before the court presents all of the same policy considerations that were present in Linklater v. Walker when this court determined not to make Matt versus O'File a result. I suppose, Mr. Martin, you had a failure in a federal criminal trial to raise something on appeal, and it's one of those grisly choice situations. Then what? Then I think you're talking about exceptional circumstances, which would have to be considered. I'm talking about the normal claim where a man comes in and says... Well, I guess you're about to say, if you're trying to use the Link Letter on these retroactive cases, you're about to say that, obviously, a search and seizure claim, then, ordinarily ought to be left to direct appeal and never be the subject of a 2255, aren't you? Well, I would say that it ought ordinarily be left to direct appeal and not the subject of 2255. Again, I would say there may be extraordinary circumstances. For example, when the failure to raise it is such that it could amount to the deprivation of counsel, and perhaps something short of that is Professor Amsterdam suggests in his article in Search and Seizure, in which he suggests that it shouldn't ordinarily lie, where there are exceptional circumstances. But I think the policy considerations articulated in Link Letter as to why you don't want to relitigate issues some substantial time after the trial. first, that memory is dim, witnesses may be lost, and I think retrial makes, one, the hearing itself difficult to determine the actual fact, and two, it makes retrial very difficult. So there are those policy considerations going. MAP also made clear that retroactive application wouldn't serve really the purpose, the deterrent purpose of the exclusionary rule. And we would submit similarly here that no purpose of the exclusionary rule would realistically be served by allowing this type of claim to be raised collaterally. I think it's clear that police officers wouldn't risk searching a car illegally, knowing that the evidence would be excluded on proper motion on the hope that perhaps it wouldn't be raised and then it couldn't be raised collaterally. I don't think that this will have any significant impact on the deterrent effect of the exclusionary rule. rule. So for these reasons, we submit that as a general rule, habeas corpus should not be allowed to test claims of illegal search and seizure absent some claim of exceptional circumstances. And I would like to now address myself to the consideration. Before I do that, I might treat briefly one other area since it has come up before the court in a procuring opinion in Jordan versus United States where the court did allow collateral attack on a matter that could have been raised in trial. That was the case where the claim was an unreasonable delay in bringing the trial, the denial of the right to a speedy trial. I think in that situation, you have no competing interest on the government side. The matter is basically determined on the record from the time. And if the relief is granted, there will not be a new trial. The case will be dismissed so that there are no finality interests really present in that type of case. And I think there, habeas corpus may lie, even though the matter could have been raised on direct appeal. Because there, the prisoner's remedy really, and right, is to be totally released from the prosecution. There will be no retrial. But I think ordinarily, where the claim is one that doesn't go to the integrity of the fact-finding process, and two, the remedy would really be to allow the prisoner a hearing, and if he prevails through the hearing, a retrial. Then I think that the interest of finality expressed in Linkletter v. Walker militate against allowing on habeas corpus the assertion of claims of such as illegal search and seizure, absent, as I said before, some extraordinary circumstances. Now, I would like to turn myself to the question whether or not there are extraordinary circumstances in this case, which would justify the grant of habeas corpus. We submit that there are not. The counsel argues that there are extraordinary circumstances because the petitioner wanted this matter raised on appeal, and it was not raised. I think first, and I think counsel candidly admitted it, although his petitioner's Kaufman's assertion that he raised this matter with counsel prior to the submission of the brief and oral argument at the original appeal, Kaufman's own letter to counsel, which appears at page 62, appended to the original brief of the petitioner, shows that he never raised the search and seizure issue with his counsel until after counsel had submitted his brief and presented oral argument. Argument was heard on March 9th, I believe. This letter was submitted to counsel April 26th. In addition, the letters of the clerk of the court also make clear, the letter set forth on page 58, the clerk of the court to Mr. Jacob, that Kaufman's letter was submitted to the panel that decided the case, Kaufman's letter citing Crest, prior to the decision of the case. So I think that it is clear that the matter did get before the panel, and we submit that the fact the panel didn't mention this issue in their opinion does not mean that they didn't consider it, but rather I would think that they agreed with petitioners of appellate counsel, who himself stated that he thought this appeal to be of little merit, this point to be of little merit. I think counsel on appeal made a deliberate choice. He looked at the search and seizure issue, found it to be of little merit, looked at the insanity questions and the issues related thereto, and determined that the best issue to raise was the insanity defense. Does the record show anything as to the caliber of the representation he had? Well, I think that the record shows, among other things, Mr. Justice Holland, one, that this man who represented him at trial was a man of some prominence in the local bar, was either at the time of trial or shortly thereafter the president of the local bar association. It also, I think, a close examination of the record at trial shows several things. One, I think that when you look at the presentation of the insanity defense, I think that it shows that petitioner was well represented. I think that counsel got the most out of the facts that were available to him. I think that the record will also show, I think, as to an examination, why counsel did not make a surgeon's seizure claim. And, in fact, support the conclusion that counsel determined that, one, the search and seizure issue meant nothing, since petitioner was going to admit the crime and his only defense was going to be insanity. And, two, that from the record as he saw it, there was really no hope of success on the search and seizure claim because, one, the searches were apparently legal, and, two, at all events, no interest of petitioner was invaded by any search of the car that occurred. Then he had another lawyer on the appeal, did he not? And he had a separate lawyer on appeal who determined... I mean, a different lawyer, not a traditional lawyer. A different lawyer. And that lawyer determined that the search and seizure issue was of no merit, also. Well, at least before the court of appeals, but then... Then, when petitioner raised it with him, he did, in submitting the petition to this court, assert it. But I think that we have here a conscious choice of counsel that the issue, particularly in light of the issue that was raised in trial and sanity, that the issue just was not worth raising. Well, Mr. Martin, based on your criteria for distinguishing between the claims that are open for 2255 and those which are not, namely whether the issue goes to the integrity of the fact-finding process, why should it help if you're not going to open up search and seizure claims for 2255, why would it help to phrase the same claim in terms of the denial of counsel? Well, I think that there... Because the only inadequacy in counsel was that he failed to raise an issue about the admission of some evidence, which is perhaps perfectly reliable evidence, and which wouldn't really go to whether or not guilt or innocence was properly determined. Well, I would think, Mr. Justice White, the problem is that if a man had counsel, which the record indicated was so inadequate, for example, if the only evidence against a defendant was illegally seized narcotics and narcotics prosecution... And he just plain... Doesn't raise it. ...fail to raise it. Then it seems to me that there is some question that the man didn't get the counsel he was entitled to in this court has basically held that counsel, the right to counsel, is retroactive at all stages of... It has held that, but it's never been focused on a particular issue like this. Well, I think that, you know, I think there may be some reason for drawing a distinction. I'm just saying that... I just don't see how your argument is any better or any worse about 2255 between counsel and...
